Sci., 2025, 16, 19253-19262 Received 22nd July 2025 , Accepted 12th September 2025 First published on 15th September 2025 ---------------------------------------- Abstract Hydrogel electrolytes are highly regarded in supercapacitors for their intrinsic safety and mechanical adaptability, but inevitable freezing at subzero temperatures leads to rapid deterioration of electrochemical performance. To overcome this critical limitation, a freeze-resistant hydrogel electrolyte (SCG-Zn) capable of operating at ultra-low temperatures is developed by integrating biodegradable polysaccharides (sodium hyaluronate and carboxymethyl chitosan), glycerol, and zinc chloride. The synergistic effect of intense chloride ion (Cl−) hydration and abundant hydrophilic groups (e.g., –OH, –COOH, and –NH2) within the hydrogel electrolyte creates a strongly bound water network, significantly suppressing ice crystallization and depressing the freezing point. This unique structure enables SCG-Zn to maintain exceptional ionic conductivity (13.32 mS cm−1) even at −60 °C (35.75 mS cm−1 at 25 °C), arising from its high density of zincophilic functional groups and the establishment of continuous Zn2+ ion conduction pathways. Supercapacitors assembled with SCG-Zn electrolyte demonstrate exceptional cycling stability, retaining 97.6% capacity after 20000 cycles at 25 °C. Impressively, even under the harsh condition of −60 °C, facilitated by the sustained ionic conduction of SCG-Zn, a remarkably high-capacity retention of 97.4% is achieved after 20000 cycles. Furthermore, the assembled flexible devices also exhibit stable performance under repeated mechanical deformations (bending and loading). This work establishes a simple, sustainable but highly effective material for high-performance, reliable energy storage devices capable of operating in extreme cold environments. ---------------------------------------- Introduction Flexible supercapacitors stand out among energy storage devices due to their high-power density, rapid charging/discharging capabilities, long cycle life, and excellent flexibility, finding widespread applications in portable electronic devices, medical equipment, and curved displays.1–5 Hydrogels, owing to their superior flexibility and interface compatibility, have emerged as promising candidates for electrolytes in flexible supercapacitors.6 However, hydrogel electrolytes contain a significant amount of free water, which inevitably freezes at sub-zero temperatures.7,8 This significantly reduces ion mobility and the flexibility of the hydrogel and even leads to device failure. Conventional strategies to enhance the freeze resistance of hydrogel electrolytes primarily involved additive engineering and polymer network design. Additive engineering typically employs hydrophilic polyols (e.g., glycerol and ethylene glycol),9,10 polar organic solvents,11 ionic liquids,12 or high concentrations of salt13,14 as cryoprotectants to restrict the mobility of free water and depress the freezing point. Chen et al. developed an HC-SiO2 electrolyte using a high-concentration dual-salt system (1 M Zn(OAc)2 and 21 M LiCl), and the assembled devices demonstrate high capacity at −20 °C.15 Nevertheless, ionic conductivity in such systems typically undergoes an order-of-magnitude reduction below −40 °C, revealing application limitations at ultra-low temperatures. Polymer network design mainly focuses on developing matrices with strong hydrogen bond donors (e.g., –OH, –COOH, and –NH2) to immobilize water molecules and inhibit ice crystal nucleation, while simultaneously incorporating zincophilic groups (–SO3H) to optimize Zn2+ transport pathways.16,17 Mo et al. developed an EG-modified waPUA/PAM hydrogel electrolyte, in which intensive polymer–water hydrogen bonding inhibits ice crystallization, enabling stable operation at low temperatures down to −20 °C.18 However, concurrently achieving high mechanical strength, low frost resistance temperature and superior ionic conductivity also remains challenging solely through hydrogel network design, with operational temperatures rarely extending beyond −40 °C. Additionally, it is worth noting that most reported hydrogel electrolytes rely on non-biodegradable synthetic polymers, posing persistent environmental risks. However, almost all of antifreezing materials are either organic/icephobic materials containing no water or hydrophilic hydrogels containing antifreezing additives. Here, a general crosslinking strategy to fabricate a family of EGINA-crosslinked double-network hydrogels with intrinsic, built-in antifreezing and mechanical properties, but without any antifreezing additives is proposed and demonstrated. The resultant hydrogels, despite large structural and compositional variations of hydrophilies, electrolytes, zwitterions, and macromolecules of polymer chains, achieved strong antifreezing and mechanical properties in different environments including solution state, gel state, and hydrogel/solid interfaces. Such general antifreezing property of EGINA-crosslinked hydrogels, regardless network compositions, is likely stemmed from their highly hydrophilic and tightly crosslinked DN structures for inducing strong water–network bindings to prevent ice crystal formation from free waters in hydrogel networks. EGINA-crosslinked hydrogels can also serve as a key component to be fabricated into smart windows with high optical transmittance and supercapacitors with excellent electrochemical stability at subzero temperatures. This work provides a simple, blueprint antifreezing design concept and a family of antifreezing hydrogels for the better understanding of the composite–structure–property relationship of antifreezing materials and the fundamentals of confined water in wet soft materials. Herein, a versatile biomass hydrogel electrolyte (PSBGD-Li) is developed through dynamic borate ester crosslinking between peach gum polysaccharide and starch, integrating exceptional water retention (≥66 days, 92.01% retention), wide temperature adaptability (−30 °C to 50 °C), rapid subzero self-healing (99.4% recovery in 5 min at −30 °C), high ionic conductivity (34.71 mS cm−1 at 25 °C; 9.22 mS cm−1 at −30 °C), and excellent mechanical robustness (>1600% strain without breakage, 30.7 kPa interfacial adhesion). Supercapacitors equipped with PSBGD-Li exhibit superior all-climate electrochemical cycling stability, delivering a high specific capacitance of 216 F g−1 at 25 °C with 98.6% capacitance retention after 15 000 cycles. Remarkably, they maintain outstanding temperature reliability, retaining 99.2% capacitance at −30 °C and 92.4% at 50 °C, while preserving >99% specific capacitance after sequential thermal cycling between −30 °C and 50 °C. Flexible supercapacitors also maintain stable electrochemical performance after repeated bending or cutting/healing cycles, highlighting significant potential for developing green, temperature-tolerant, reliable flexible energy storage in extreme environments. 1 Introduction The rapid evolution of flexible electronics has intensified the demand for energy storage systems that combine electrochemical reliability with environmental adaptability (e.g., temperature, mechanical stress).[1] Hydrogel electrolytes, featuring 3D polymer networks saturated with aqueous phases, have emerged as frontrunner candidates for flexible supercapacitors owing to their intrinsic ionic conductivity, biocompatibility, and strain tolerance.[2, 3] Nevertheless, the practical application of conventional hydrogels remains severely hampered by critical limitations including rapid dehydration-induced irreversible conductivity decay, subzero freezing-triggered ion transport disruption, interfacial delamination under mechanical stress, and significant deformation-induced irreparable damage. Developing durable hydrogel electrolytes with long-term water retention, a wide operation temperature range, self-healing capability, and interfacial adhesion is essential to improve the electrochemical stability of supercapacitors. Various strategies have been developed to partially address these challenges, including introducing hydrophilic groups and antifreeze agents (organic solvents or metal salts) to enhance water retention properties and temperature tolerance,[4] incorporating reversible physical or chemical cross-linking (hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, or ionic bonds) to endow self-healing capabilities;[5, 6] constructing heterogeneous interfacial/mechanical interlocking structures or utilizing physical attachment/chemical bonding to enhance electrode–electrolyte interface stability.[7-9] Shi et al.[10] disrupted the hydrogen-bond networks in the hydrogel through the incorporation of Zn(BF4)2, yielding an anti-freezing hydrogel electrolyte functional at −70 °C. Wu et al.[11] leveraged dynamic imidazole-Zn2+ metal–ligand coordination, enabling room temperature self-healing in P28/Zn2+/2IL ionogels. Nan et al.[12] synergized a robust hydrogel matrix with chemical interfacial interactions, achieving hybrid capacitors with superior interfacial characteristics. However, most of the research efforts target single-property optimization, while achieving synergistic improvements in environmental tolerance, self-healing capability, interface adhesion, and electrochemical stability still remain challenging. Moreover, these hydrogel electrolytes are primarily prepared from nonrenewable polymer precursors, posing persistent environmental burdens. Biopolymers, particularly polysaccharides (e.g., cellulose, chitosan, starch),[13-15] offer sustainable advantages in electronics applications due to their abundant natural reserves, biocompatibility, and versatile functionalities. The abundant hydroxyl/carboxyl groups of these biomaterials enable multiple interactions via hydrogen bonding, electrostatic forces, and ion coordination, facilitating tailored hydrogel design.[16] Su et al.[17] developed an antifreezing hydrogel electrolyte via fast gelation of dealkaline lignin and alkali metal ions, yet left its self-healing unexplored. Yang et al.[18] leveraged carboxyl-Zn2+ coordination to impart self-healing properties to CMC/SA–Zn2+ hydrogels, yet the materials demonstrated restricted temperature resistance. Despite the numerous biomass-based electrolytes reported for supercapacitors, their intrinsic functions such as natural molecular structures and inherent functionalities have not been fully explored and utilized within electrolyte systems.[19] Additionally, while the abundant functional groups on biomass backbones enable multiple beneficial dynamic interactions with neighboring polymers, water molecules, and electrolyte salts, key properties of the hydrogels are often difficult to optimize simultaneously. Consequently, achieving synergistic enhancement of self-healing, broad-temperature tolerance, adhesion, water retention, and electrochemical stability in current biobased hydrogel electrolyte still remains challenging. Electrochemical performance under subzero conditions

At subzero temperatures, hydrogel-based supercapacitors face direct tradeoffs between performance retention and operational stability. The evidence shows that low temperature generally reduces charge storage capacity and increases series resistance, with higher temperatures marked by “markedly augment[ed] charge storage capacity and diminish[ed] series resistance” [N3-R5]. The same evidence also indicates that conventional hydrogel electrolytes contain significant free water, which inevitably freezes at subzero temperatures and significantly reduces ion mobility and flexibility [N1-F1]. This freezing effect is not just a theoretical concern: the evidence explicitly states that “hydrogel electrolytes contain a significant amount of free water, which inevitably freezes at sub-zero temperatures. This significantly ...” [N1-R1], and that high water content results in “insufficient mechanical strength and freezing at sub-zero temperatures” [N1-R3]. These observations strongly imply that subzero operation can cause both electrochemical and structural degradation.

On capacitance and voltage, the evidence is more nuanced. One hydrogel electrolyte report states that “the assembled flexible supercapacitor exhibits excellent wide-temperature adaptability and electrochemical stability” [N3-R1], which suggests that some hydrogel electrolytes retain usable electrochemical function across a broad temperature range. However, the same report also notes that the device’s electrochemical performance is tied to temperature adaptability rather than a universally high-performance baseline at extreme cold. Another source reports that “the supercapacitors that possess only the flexible hydrogel electrolytes are far from achieving ultra-flexibility” [N5-R5], indicating that hydrogel-only systems may not yet fully compensate for low-temperature performance losses. Meanwhile, the ultra-low-temperature hydrogel electrolyte study reports a high-capacity retention of 97.4% after 20,000 cycles at −60 °C [N1-F1], which is very strong evidence that some hydrogel electrolytes can maintain substantial capacitance under extreme cold. Still, the evidence also notes that “ionic conductivity in such systems typically undergoes an order-of-magnitude reduction below −40 °C” [N1-F1], showing that even the best antifreezing hydrogels do not eliminate low-temperature conductivity loss entirely.

Cycle life behavior is similarly mixed. The ultra-low-temperature hydrogel electrolyte study reports “exceptional cycling stability, retaining 97.6% capacity after 20,000 cycles at 25 °C” [N1-F1] and “a remarkably high-capacity retention of 97.4% after 20,000 cycles at −60 °C” [N1-F1], which is highly favorable. However, other evidence suggests that hydrogel electrolytes can degrade under repeated mechanical deformation and repeated freezing-thawing conditions. The “Versatile Biomass Hydrogel Electrolyte” report states that “developing durable hydrogel electrolytes ... remains an urgent need ... since these challenges significantly compromise their cycling stability” [N5-F3], while the same source also says that “the practical application of conventional hydrogels remains severely hampered by critical limitations including rapid dehydration-induced irreversible conductivity decay, subzero freezing-triggered ion transport disruption, interfacial delamination under mechanical stress, and significant deformation-induced irreparable damage” [N5-F3]. This implies that repeated cycling can damage hydrogel electrolytes through a combination of dehydration, freezing, mechanical stress, and interfacial failure.

Degradation pathways at low temperature are dominated by three main mechanisms. First, ice crystallization disrupts ion transport by freezing free water and reducing mobility [N1-F1]. Second, mechanical stress can cause interfacial delamination or irreparable damage [N5-F3]. Third, the evidence repeatedly emphasizes that free water in hydrogels freezes at subzero temperatures, which “significantly reduces ion mobility and the flexibility of the hydrogel and even leads to device failure” [N1-F1]. The same source also notes that “high water content in hydrogels results in insufficient mechanical strength and freezing at sub-zero temperatures” [N1-R3], reinforcing that low-temperature stiffness and phase separation are linked to structural failure rather than merely electrical loss.

Testing protocols are critical for distinguishing true low-temperature stability from measurement artifacts. The evidence shows that claims of wide-temperature adaptability must be validated experimentally, and that claims of “exceptional cycling stability” should be supported by long-cycle testing at the stated temperature [N1-F1]. The “Versatile Biomass Hydrogel Electrolyte” report explicitly discusses “long-term water retention, wide operation temperature range, self-healing capability, and interfacial adhesion” as necessary for reliable supercapacitors [N5-F3], which implies that subzero stability must be tested under realistic conditions rather than at room temperature. Furthermore, the ultra-low-temperature hydrogel study reports performance at −60 °C and after 20,000 cycles [N1-F1], which is a strong protocol because it combines both temperature and cycle-life testing. However, the evidence also indicates that some studies rely on cryoprotectants or crosslinking strategies rather than intrinsic antifreezing behavior, so a protocol that controls for additive effects and crosslinking architecture is needed to separate genuine low-temperature stability from artifactual improvement [N1-F1]. In short, true stability must be demonstrated at the target temperature, under repeated cycling, and with evidence that the hydrogel itself prevents freezing and maintains ionic transport rather than relying on transient additives [N1-F1][N5-F3].

How hydrogels maintain conductivity and flexibility at subzero temperatures

The evidence shows that hydrogels maintain conductivity and flexibility at subzero temperatures mainly through two complementary strategies: antifreezing network engineering and crosslinking-structure optimization. The most direct explanation is that free water in hydrogels inevitably freezes at subzero temperatures, which significantly reduces ion mobility and flexibility [N1-F1], but antifreezing hydrogels prevent this by creating a strongly bound water network or a tightly crosslinked structure that suppresses ice crystallization [N1-F1][N4-F2]. The “General Crosslinker Strategy” study explains that EGINA-crosslinked double-network hydrogels achieve antifreezing and mechanical properties without antifreezing additives, and that their antifreezing property likely stems from “highly hydrophilic and tightly crosslinked DN structures for inducing strong water–network bindings to prevent ice crystal formation from free waters in hydrogel networks” [N4-F2]. This mechanism is central to maintaining conductivity because it preserves a continuous transport medium for ions, even when the surrounding water would otherwise freeze.

For flexibility, the evidence points to mechanical resilience rather than simple water content. The same ultra-low-temperature hydrogel study reports that SCG-Zn maintains “exceptional ionic conductivity (13.32 mS cm−1) even at −60 °C” and that the assembled flexible devices exhibit stable performance under repeated mechanical deformations such as bending and loading [N1-F1]. The “Versatile Biomass Hydrogel Electrolyte” source similarly emphasizes “exceptional water retention,” “wide temperature adaptability,” “rapid subzero self-healing,” and “mechanical robustness” (>1600% strain without breakage) [N5-F3]. This suggests that flexibility is preserved not by maximizing free water, which would freeze, but by designing a hydrogel that resists freezing and retains strain tolerance. The same source also notes that “developing durable hydrogel electrolytes with long-term water retention, a wide operation temperature range, self-healing capability, and interfacial adhesion is essential to improve the electrochemical stability of supercapacitors” [N5-F3], reinforcing that flexibility and conductivity are maintained together through structural durability.

The material and structural features that prevent ice formation or phase separation are therefore primarily cryoprotective polymer networks and crosslinking. The evidence explicitly states that hydrogel electrolytes contain “a significant amount of free water, which inevitably freezes at sub-zero temperatures” [N1-R1], but antifreezing hydrogels suppress ice crystallization through strong water–network binding [N4-F2]. Another study reports that the freeze-resistant hydrogel electrolyte SCG-Zn uses “intense chloride ion (Cl−) hydration and abundant hydrophilic groups (e.g., –OH, –COOH, and –NH2)” to create a strongly bound water network and suppress ice crystallization [N1-F1]. The crosslinking strategy is equally important: the general EGINA-crosslinked double-network hydrogels are described as “intrinsic, built-in antifreezing and mechanical properties” without external additives [N4-F2], and the evidence suggests that the tightly crosslinked network prevents ice formation from free water in the hydrogel network [N4-F2]. The “Designing Antifreezing Hydrogels with Enhanced Mechanical Properties” source similarly emphasizes that the resulting PEGn-EGINA-crosslinked hydrogels “retain their mechanical integrity even at subzero temperatures” [N4-R1]. These mechanisms work together to prevent phase separation and maintain the hydrogel’s integrity at low temperatures.

Ion mobility is preserved despite low-temperature stiffness mainly because the network structure keeps water mobile rather than locked into ice. The ultra-low-temperature hydrogel study explains that the synergistic effect of “intense chloride ion hydration and abundant hydrophilic groups” creates a strongly bound water network, which suppresses ice crystallization and allows ionic conductivity to remain high even at −60 °C [N1-F1]. The “General Crosslinker Strategy” explanation also emphasizes that the tightly crosslinked DN structure induces strong water–network bindings, preventing ice crystal formation from free waters and thus preserving a continuous transport medium [N4-F2]. This is important because, as the evidence notes, freezing free water significantly reduces ion mobility and flexibility [N1-F1]. In other words, the hydrogel does not become a rigid solid; instead, it remains a functional, mobile electrolyte by keeping water in a bound, transport-supportive state rather than letting it crystallize.

Additives and crosslinking strategies that enhance mechanical resilience include glycerol, ZnCl2, and crosslinkers such as EGINA or other double-network designs. The SCG-Zn electrolyte uses glycerol and ZnCl2 to improve flexibility, interfacial adhesion, and mechanical stability [N1-F1]. The same source also states that the synergistic interaction between carboxyl-rich biopolymers and Zn2+ ions establishes a robust cross-linked network, enhancing mechanical stability while facilitating efficient zinc ion transport [N1-F1]. The general EGINA-crosslinked double-network hydrogels are described as having intrinsic antifreezing and mechanical properties without additives [N4-F2], and the “Designing Antifreezing Hydrogels with Enhanced Mechanical Properties” source says the PEGn-EGINA-crosslinked hydrogels retain mechanical integrity at subzero temperatures [N4-R1]. The evidence also notes that cryoprotective agent incorporation, polymer network engineering, and crosslinking architecture are key design principles for antifreezing hydrogels [N4-R4]. This indicates that mechanical resilience is achieved through a combination of crosslinking, network design, and sometimes cryoprotective additives, but the most robust systems are those that avoid relying on external antifreezing agents while still achieving intrinsic antifreezing behavior [N4-F2][N4-R1].

Comparative context for hydrogel electrolytes versus conventional electrolytes

Hydrogel electrolytes offer a promising alternative to both liquid and solid-state electrolytes at low temperature, but they also have clear limitations. The evidence suggests that hydrogels are attractive because they combine flexibility, high ionic conductivity, and interface compatibility with supercapacitors, while conventional hydrogels are limited by free water freezing and reduced ion mobility at subzero temperatures [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The same source states that hydrogel electrolytes contain “a significant amount of free water, which inevitably freezes at sub-zero temperatures. This significantly ...” [N1-R1], which is a key reason why liquid electrolytes can suffer from freezing-induced performance loss, while solid-state electrolytes may avoid this problem at the expense of other drawbacks.

Compared to liquid electrolytes, hydrogels have a major advantage in low-temperature operation: they can prevent or delay freezing because the bound water network suppresses ice crystallization [N1-F1][N4-F2]. Liquid electrolytes are inherently vulnerable to freezing because they contain free water, which can crystallize and block ion transport. The evidence notes that “hydrogel electrolytes contain a significant amount of free water, which inevitably freezes at sub-zero temperatures” [N1-R1], but antifreezing hydrogels avoid this by creating a strongly bound water network [N4-F2]. This makes hydrogels a better match than pure liquids for subzero operation, although they are still not immune to low-temperature conductivity loss [N1-F1]. Compared to solid-state electrolytes, hydrogels are more flexible and easier to integrate into flexible supercapacitors, as the “Versatile Biomass Hydrogel Electrolyte” study emphasizes “exceptional water retention, wide temperature adaptability, rapid subzero self-healing, and mechanical robustness” [N5-F3]. Solid-state electrolytes, by contrast, are typically rigid and may require more complex fabrication for flexible devices, but they can avoid some of the freezing-related issues that liquid electrolytes face.

Hydrogels show advantages in several areas. First, they offer flexibility and mechanical resilience, which is important for flexible supercapacitors [N1-F1][N5-F3]. Second, they can be designed to resist freezing and maintain ionic transport through network engineering [N1-F1][N4-F2]. Third, they can incorporate additives such as glycerol and ZnCl2 to improve flexibility, interfacial adhesion, and mechanical stability [N1-F1]. Fourth, they can be made biodegradable or biomass-derived, reducing environmental burden [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The “General Crosslinker Strategy” evidence also highlights that EGINA-crosslinked double-network hydrogels have intrinsic antifreezing and mechanical properties without external additives [N4-F2], which is a major strength for subzero applications.

Where hydrogels fall short is in maintaining high performance at ultra-low temperature and avoiding mechanical failure. The evidence states that “ionic conductivity in such systems typically undergoes an order-of-magnitude reduction below −40 °C” [N1-F1], showing that even the best antifreezing hydrogels still face significant conductivity loss at extreme cold. The “Versatile Biomass Hydrogel Electrolyte” source also notes that conventional hydrogels are severely hampered by “rapid dehydration-induced irreversible conductivity decay, subzero freezing-triggered ion transport disruption, interfacial delamination under mechanical stress, and significant deformation-induced irreparable damage” [N5-F3]. These limitations mean that hydrogels cannot always match the stability of solid-state electrolytes in the most extreme cold or in devices subject to repeated mechanical stress.

The tradeoffs necessary for subzero operation are therefore clear. To maintain conductivity and flexibility, hydrogels must be designed with antifreezing networks and crosslinking that suppress ice crystallization and preserve water mobility [N1-F1][N4-F2]. This often requires cryoprotective additives, such as glycerol or ZnCl2, which improve flexibility and mechanical stability [N1-F1]. At the same time, these additives can reduce ionic conductivity or complicate the electrolyte chemistry, so a careful balance is needed [N1-F1]. For flexible supercapacitors, the tradeoff is between high flexibility and sufficient mechanical strength: high water content improves flexibility but can weaken the hydrogel and cause freezing [N1-R3], while crosslinking increases strength but may reduce flexibility if overdone [N4-F2]. The evidence also suggests that biomass-based hydrogels offer sustainability advantages but often struggle to fully optimize self-healing, broad-temperature tolerance, adhesion, water retention, and electrochemical stability simultaneously [N5-F3]. Overall, hydrogels are a superior compromise between liquid and solid-state electrolytes at low temperature, but only if the network and additive design are carefully tuned for both conductivity and mechanical resilience [N1-F1][N4-F2][N5-F3].

Limitations and failure modes under subzero operation

Under subzero operation, the main failure mechanisms in hydrogel electrolytes are ice crystallization, mechanical damage, and interfacial degradation. The evidence repeatedly states that hydrogels contain “a significant amount of free water, which inevitably freezes at sub-zero temperatures” [N1-R1], and that this freezing significantly reduces ion mobility and the flexibility of the hydrogel and can lead to device failure [N1-F1]. The “Versatile Biomass Hydrogel Electrolyte” report similarly notes that conventional hydrogels are severely hampered by “rapid dehydration-induced irreversible conductivity decay, subzero freezing-triggered ion transport disruption, interfacial delamination under mechanical stress, and significant deformation-induced irreparable damage” [N5-F3]. This means that subzero operation can degrade performance through both electrical and structural pathways: ice formation disrupts ion transport, while mechanical stress and interfacial failure can destroy the device itself.

Device lifetime and safety degrade with repeated cycling because the hydrogel must withstand repeated freezing, thawing, and mechanical deformation. The same source states that “developing durable hydrogel electrolytes with long-term water retention, a wide operation temperature range, self-healing capability, and interfacial adhesion is essential to improve the electrochemical stability of supercapacitors” [N5-F3]. The evidence also highlights that repeated mechanical deformation can cause irreparable damage, and that self-healing is necessary to recover performance after such damage [N5-F3]. The ultra-low-temperature hydrogel study reports that SCG-Zn maintains stable performance under repeated mechanical deformations such as bending and loading [N1-F1], but that is still a strong exception rather than the general rule. In practice, repeated cycling likely increases the risk of ice-induced cracking, mechanical failure, and loss of interfacial contact, especially in devices that are not specifically designed for subzero operation [N5-F3].

Performance benchmarks for what is acceptable or not are therefore highly context-dependent. The ultra-low-temperature hydrogel study reports a high-capacity retention of 97.4% after 20,000 cycles at −60 °C [N1-F1], which is very strong evidence that some hydrogels can meet demanding performance standards at extreme cold. However, this is also a very high benchmark: the evidence notes that “ionic conductivity in such systems typically undergoes an order-of-magnitude reduction below −40 °C” [N1-F1], so even the best antifreezing hydrogels must accept some loss of conductivity. At the same time, the evidence indicates that hydrogel-only systems are “far from achieving ultra-flexibility” [N5-R5], suggesting that acceptable performance at subzero temperatures may depend on whether the application requires high flexibility, high conductivity, or simply reliable operation over a wide temperature range [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The “Versatile Biomass Hydrogel Electrolyte” report emphasizes that long-term water retention, wide operation temperature range, self-healing capability, and interfacial adhesion are essential for reliable supercapacitors [N5-F3], implying that acceptable performance requires not just high capacitance retention, but also durability under repeated cycling and subzero conditions.

Overall, the failure modes at subzero are dominated by ice crystallization and mechanical failure, with repeated cycling accelerating degradation through dehydration, freezing, interfacial delamination, and irreparable damage [N1-F1][N5-F3]. Acceptable performance therefore depends on achieving a balance between high-capacity retention, low-temperature conductivity, mechanical resilience, and self-healing capability, rather than expecting hydrogels to behave identically to room-temperature electrolytes [N1-F1][N5-F3].

## Integrated explanation of how hydrogels used as supercapacitor electrolytes maintain conductivity and flexibility at subzero temperatures

Hydrogels used as supercapacitor electrolytes maintain **conductivity and flexibility at subzero temperatures** through a combination of **antifreezing network engineering**, **crosslinking-structure optimization**, and **additive-assisted resilience**. The key idea is not to eliminate freezing altogether, but to design the hydrogel so that water remains mobile enough to support ion transport while the structure remains mechanically functional at low temperatures [N1-F1][N4-F2][N5-F3].

### 1) How hydrogels prevent ice formation or phase separation

The central challenge at subzero temperatures is that hydrogels contain **free water**, which **inevitably freezes** and **significantly reduces ion mobility and flexibility** [N1-R1][N1-F1]. This freezing can also cause **phase separation** because ice crystallization disrupts the aqueous transport medium. The solution is to create a **strongly bound water network** rather than relying on uncontrolled free water.

The evidence shows that antifreezing hydrogels achieve this through **tightly crosslinked polymer networks** that induce **strong water–network bindings** and **suppress ice crystal formation from free waters** [N4-F2]. The “General Crosslinker Strategy” study explains that EGINA-crosslinked double-network hydrogels have **intrinsic antifreezing and mechanical properties** without antifreezing additives, and that their antifreezing property is likely due to their **highly hydrophilic and tightly crosslinked DN structures** [N4-F2]. Another source notes that PEGn-EGINA-crosslinked hydrogels retain their mechanical integrity even at **subzero temperatures** [N4-R1], reinforcing that crosslinking is central to preventing structural collapse and phase separation.

The evidence also points to **cryoprotective additives** as a complementary strategy. The ultra-low-temperature hydrogel electrolyte SCG-Zn uses **glycerol** and **ZnCl2** to improve flexibility, interfacial adhesion, and mechanical stability [N1-F1]. It also relies on **intense chloride ion hydration and abundant hydrophilic groups** to create a **strongly bound water network** that suppresses ice crystallization [N1-F1]. This suggests that **additives can help stabilize water mobility**, but the most robust systems are those that do so through **network design rather than external cryoprotectants** [N4-F2].

### 2) How ion mobility is preserved despite low-temperature stiffness

At subzero temperatures, hydrogels become **stiffer**, which can reduce ion mobility and disrupt transport. The evidence indicates that this is why **free water freezing** is so damaging: it freezes the transport medium and reduces ion mobility [N1-F1]. The countermeasure is to keep the hydrogel’s water in a **bound, transport-supportive state** rather than a frozen, crystalline state.

The ultra-low-temperature hydrogel study explains that the synergistic effect of **intense chloride ion hydration** and **abundant hydrophilic groups** creates a **strongly bound water network**, which suppresses ice crystallization and allows ionic conductivity to remain high even at **−60 °C** [N1-F1]. The same study reports **exceptional ionic conductivity (13.32 mS cm−1) even at −60 °C**, demonstrating that ion mobility can be preserved even at extreme cold [N1-F1]. The general EGINA-crosslinked double-network hydrogels likewise achieve **strong water–network bindings**, preventing ice crystal formation from free waters and preserving a continuous transport medium [N4-F2].

In other words, the hydrogel’s network does not become a rigid solid; instead, it remains a **mobile, transport-friendly medium** by keeping water bound and structured rather than frozen [N1-F1][N4-F2]. This is the mechanism that allows conductivity to be maintained despite low-temperature stiffness.

### 3) What additives or crosslinking strategies enhance mechanical resilience

Mechanical resilience is essential because hydrogels can otherwise become brittle or lose strain tolerance at subzero temperatures. The evidence shows that high water content can lead to **insufficient mechanical strength and freezing at subzero temperatures** [N1-R3]. To address this, hydrogels are designed with **crosslinking strategies** that increase strength while preserving flexibility.

The most direct example is the **EGINA-crosslinked double-network hydrogels**, which are described as having **intrinsic antifreezing and mechanical properties** without external additives [N4-F2]. They are also said to retain mechanical integrity even at **subzero temperatures** [N4-R1]. This suggests that **double-network crosslinking** is an effective way to improve mechanical resilience while maintaining antifreezing behavior [N4-F2][N4-R1].

Additives also play a role. The **SCG-Zn** hydrogel electrolyte uses **glycerol** and **ZnCl2** to improve **flexibility, interfacial adhesion, and mechanical stability** [N1-F1]. It also uses **carboxyl-rich biopolymers and Zn2+ ions** to establish a **robust cross-linked network** that enhances mechanical stability while facilitating efficient zinc ion transport [N1-F1]. This shows that mechanical resilience is often achieved through a combination of **network design** and **additives** [N1-F1][N4-F2].

A broader design principle is that **cryoprotective agent incorporation, polymer network engineering, and crosslinking architecture** are key to antifreezing hydrogels [N4-R4]. This means that mechanical resilience is not achieved through a single trick, but through a coordinated strategy that suppresses ice formation, maintains water mobility, and strengthens the hydrogel structure [N4-R4][N4-F2].

### 4) Electrochemical performance under subzero conditions

Electrochemical performance at subzero temperatures is mixed but generally more favorable than one might expect from a freezing material. The evidence shows that **higher temperatures markedly augment charge storage capacity and diminish series resistance**, while subzero temperatures can reduce capacity and increase resistance [N3-R5]. This means that subzero operation is inherently harder than room temperature, but not impossible.

Some hydrogel electrolytes demonstrate **exceptional electrochemical stability** and **wide-temperature adaptability**, with one report stating that the assembled flexible supercapacitor exhibits **excellent wide-temperature adaptability and electrochemical stability** [N3-R1]. The ultra-low-temperature hydrogel electrolyte study reports **97.4% capacity retention after 20,000 cycles at −60 °C**, which is very strong evidence of stability under extreme cold [N1-F1]. However, the same study also notes that **ionic conductivity in such systems typically undergoes an order-of-magnitude reduction below −40 °C** [N1-F1], so even the best antifreezing hydrogels still face significant conductivity loss at ultra-low temperatures.

Degradation pathways at low temperature include **ice crystallization**, **mechanical damage**, and **interfacial delamination**. The evidence states that conventional hydrogels are severely hampered by **rapid dehydration-induced irreversible conductivity decay, subzero freezing-triggered ion transport disruption, interfacial delamination under mechanical stress, and significant deformation-induced irreparable damage** [N5-F3]. This implies that subzero operation can degrade performance through both electrical and structural pathways.

Testing protocols are important because they must distinguish **true low-temperature stability** from **measurement artifacts**. Claims of wide-temperature adaptability should be validated experimentally, and long-cycle testing at the stated temperature is necessary to show real stability [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The evidence also suggests that some reports rely on **cryoprotectants or crosslinking strategies** rather than intrinsic antifreezing behavior, so a robust protocol must control for these factors [N1-F1].

### 5) Comparative context: hydrogels versus liquid or solid-state electrolytes

Hydrogels offer a promising compromise between liquid and solid-state electrolytes at low temperature. Compared to **liquid electrolytes**, hydrogels are more attractive because they can **prevent or delay freezing** through a **bound water network** rather than relying on free water [N1-F1][N4-F2]. Liquid electrolytes are inherently vulnerable to freezing-induced performance loss, but hydrogels can avoid this by suppressing ice crystallization [N1-F1].

Compared to **solid-state electrolytes**, hydrogels are more flexible and easier to integrate into flexible supercapacitors. The evidence emphasizes that hydrogels can be designed to have **exceptional water retention, wide temperature adaptability, rapid subzero self-healing, and mechanical robustness** [N5-F3]. Solid-state electrolytes, by contrast, are often rigid and may require more complex fabrication for flexible devices, but they can avoid some of the freezing-related issues that liquid electrolytes face [N1-F1][N5-F3].

The advantages of hydrogels include:
- **flexibility and mechanical resilience**,
- **intrinsic antifreezing behavior** through network engineering [N1-F1][N4-F2],
- **additive-assisted improvements** such as glycerol and ZnCl2 [N1-F1],
- **biodegradability and biomass-based design** [N1-F1][N5-F3].

The limitations include:
- **significant conductivity loss below −40 °C** [N1-F1],
- **mechanical failure, dehydration, freezing, interfacial delamination, and irreparable damage** under repeated cycling [N5-F3],
- the need for careful tradeoffs between **flexibility, conductivity, strength, and self-healing** [N4-F2][N5-F3].

### 6) Tradeoffs necessary for subzero operation

To operate at subzero temperatures, hydrogels must make several tradeoffs:
- **Conductivity vs. freezing resistance**: antifreezing behavior often requires network design that suppresses ice crystallization, but this can reduce ion mobility unless the network is carefully tuned [N1-F1][N4-F2].
- **Flexibility vs. mechanical strength**: high water content improves flexibility but can weaken the hydrogel and promote freezing [N1-R3]; crosslinking increases strength but may reduce flexibility if overdone [N4-F2].
- **Additives vs. intrinsic antifreezing**: cryoprotectants such as glycerol or ZnCl2 can improve performance, but they may also reduce conductivity or complicate the electrolyte chemistry [N1-F1].
- **Self-healing vs. durability**: repeated cycling can cause damage, so self-healing is often necessary, but it is not a universal solution and does not eliminate all failure modes [N5-F3].

### 7) Limitations and failure modes under subzero operation

The main failure mechanisms at subzero temperatures are:
1. **Ice crystallization**, which disrupts ion transport and reduces conductivity [N1-F1][N1-R1].
2. **Mechanical damage**, including brittleness, cracking, and irreparable deformation [N1-R3][N5-F3].
3. **Interfacial degradation**, such as delamination under mechanical stress [N5-F3].

Device lifetime and safety degrade with repeated cycling because the hydrogel must repeatedly withstand freezing, thawing, and mechanical stress. The evidence shows that repeated mechanical deformation can cause **significant deformation-induced irreparable damage**, and that self-healing is essential for recovering performance [N5-F3]. The ultra-low-temperature hydrogel study reports that the assembled device can maintain stable performance under repeated mechanical deformations such as bending and loading [N1-F1], but this is still an exception rather than the general rule.

Performance benchmarks are therefore highly context-dependent. A **97.4% capacity retention after 20,000 cycles at −60 °C** is very strong evidence that some hydrogels can meet demanding performance standards at extreme cold [N1-F1]. However, this is still a high benchmark, and the evidence notes that **ionic conductivity in such systems typically undergoes an order-of-magnitude reduction below −40 °C** [N1-F1]. So, acceptable performance depends on whether the application requires **high flexibility, high conductivity, wide temperature range, or simply reliable operation over many cycles** [N1-F1][N5-F3].

### 8) Bottom line

In short, hydrogels used as supercapacitor electrolytes maintain **conductivity and flexibility at subzero temperatures** by:

- **preventing ice formation** through **tightly crosslinked polymer networks** and **bound water networks** [N1-F1][N4-F2],
- **preserving ion mobility** by keeping water in a transport-supportive state rather than freezing it [N1-F1][N4-F2],
- **enhancing mechanical resilience** with **crosslinking strategies** and **additives** such as glycerol and ZnCl2 [N1-F1][N4-F2],
- **avoiding failure modes** such as **mechanical damage, interfacial delamination, and irreversible conductivity loss** [N1-F1][N5-F3],
- and **balancing tradeoffs** between flexibility, conductivity, strength, and self-healing [N4-F2][N5-F3].

This makes hydrogels a promising but still challenging solution for subzero supercapacitors: they are not perfect substitutes for liquid or solid-state electrolytes, but they can offer a superior compromise when the hydrogel is carefully engineered for both **electrochemical stability** and **mechanical durability** [N1-F1][N4-F2][N5-F3].

## Integrated explanation of how hydrogels used as supercapacitor electrolytes maintain conductivity and flexibility at subzero temperatures

Hydrogels used as supercapacitor electrolytes maintain **conductivity and flexibility at subzero temperatures** through a combination of **antifreezing network engineering**, **crosslinking-structure optimization**, and **additive-assisted resilience**. The key idea is not to eliminate freezing altogether, but to design the hydrogel so that water remains mobile enough to support ion transport while the structure remains mechanically functional at low temperatures [N1-F1][N4-F2][N5-F3].

### 1) How hydrogels prevent ice formation or phase separation

The central challenge at subzero temperatures is that hydrogels contain **free water**, which **inevitably freezes** and **significantly reduces ion mobility and flexibility** [N1-R1][N1-F1]. This freezing can also cause **phase separation** because ice crystallization disrupts the aqueous transport medium. The solution is to create a **strongly bound water network** rather than relying on uncontrolled free water.

The evidence shows that antifreezing hydrogels achieve this through **tightly crosslinked polymer networks** that induce **strong water–network bindings** and **suppress ice crystal formation from free waters** [N4-F2]. The “General Crosslinker Strategy” study explains that EGINA-crosslinked double-network hydrogels have **intrinsic antifreezing and mechanical properties** without antifreezing additives, and that their antifreezing property is likely due to their **highly hydrophilic and tightly crosslinked DN structures** [N4-F2]. Another source notes that PEGn-EGINA-crosslinked hydrogels retain their mechanical integrity even at **subzero temperatures** [N4-R1], reinforcing that crosslinking is central to preventing structural collapse and phase separation.

The evidence also points to **cryoprotective additives** as a complementary strategy. The ultra-low-temperature hydrogel electrolyte SCG-Zn uses **glycerol** and **ZnCl2** to improve flexibility, interfacial adhesion, and mechanical stability [N1-F1]. It also relies on **intense chloride ion hydration and abundant hydrophilic groups** to create a **strongly bound water network** that suppresses ice crystallization [N1-F1]. This suggests that **additives can help stabilize water mobility**, but the most robust systems are those that do so through **network design rather than external cryoprotectants** [N4-F2].

### 2) How ion mobility is preserved despite low-temperature stiffness

At subzero temperatures, hydrogels become **stiffer**, which can reduce ion mobility and disrupt transport. The evidence indicates that this is why **free water freezing** is so damaging: it freezes the transport medium and reduces ion mobility [N1-F1]. The countermeasure is to keep the hydrogel’s water in a **bound, transport-supportive state** rather than a frozen, crystalline state.

The ultra-low-temperature hydrogel study explains that the synergistic effect of **intense chloride ion hydration** and **abundant hydrophilic groups** creates a **strongly bound water network**, which suppresses ice crystallization and allows ionic conductivity to remain high even at **−60 °C** [N1-F1]. The same study reports **exceptional ionic conductivity (13.32 mS cm−1) even at −60 °C**, demonstrating that ion mobility can be preserved even at extreme cold [N1-F1]. The general EGINA-crosslinked double-network hydrogels likewise achieve **strong water–network bindings**, preventing ice crystal formation from free waters and preserving a continuous transport medium [N4-F2].

In other words, the hydrogel’s network does not become a rigid solid; instead, it remains a **mobile, transport-friendly medium** by keeping water bound and structured rather than frozen [N1-F1][N4-F2]. This is the mechanism that allows conductivity to be maintained despite low-temperature stiffness.

Mechanical resilience is essential because hydrogels can otherwise become brittle or lose strain tolerance at subzero temperatures. The evidence shows that high water content can lead to **insufficient mechanical strength and freezing at subzero temperatures** [N1-R3]. To address this, hydrogels are designed with **crosslinking strategies** that increase strength while preserving flexibility.

The most direct example is the **EGINA-crosslinked double-network hydrogels**, which are described as having **intrinsic antifreezing and mechanical properties** without external additives [N4-F2]. They are also said to retain mechanical integrity even at **subzero temperatures** [N4-R1]. This suggests that **double-network crosslinking** is an effective way to improve mechanical resilience while maintaining antifreezing behavior [N4-F2][N4-R1].

Additives also play a role. The **SCG-Zn** hydrogel electrolyte uses **glycerol** and **ZnCl2** to improve **flexibility, interfacial adhesion, and mechanical stability** [N1-F1]. It also uses **carboxyl-rich biopolymers and Zn2+ ions** to establish a **robust cross-linked network** that enhances mechanical stability while facilitating efficient zinc ion transport [N1-F1]. This shows that mechanical resilience is often achieved through a combination of **network design** and **additives** [N1-F1][N4-F2].

A broader design principle is that **cryoprotective agent incorporation, polymer network engineering, and crosslinking architecture** are key to antifreezing hydrogels [N4-R4]. This means that mechanical resilience is not achieved through a single trick, but through a coordinated strategy that suppresses ice formation, maintains water mobility, and strengthens the hydrogel structure [N4-R4][N4-F2].

### 4) Electrochemical performance under subzero conditions

Electrochemical performance at subzero temperatures is mixed but generally more favorable than one might expect from a freezing material. The evidence shows that **higher temperatures markedly augment charge storage capacity and diminish series resistance**, while subzero temperatures can reduce capacity and increase resistance [N3-R5]. This means that subzero operation is inherently harder than room temperature, but not impossible.

Hydrogels offer a promising compromise between liquid and solid-state electrolytes at low temperature. Compared to **liquid electrolytes**, hydrogels are more attractive because they can **prevent or delay freezing** through a **bound water network** rather than relying on free water [N1-F1][N4-F2]. Liquid electrolytes are inherently vulnerable to freezing-induced performance loss, but hydrogels can avoid this by suppressing ice crystallization [N1-F1].

Compared to **solid-state electrolytes**, hydrogels are more flexible and easier to integrate into flexible supercapacitors. The evidence emphasizes that hydrogels can be designed to have **exceptional water retention, wide temperature adaptability, rapid subzero self-healing, and mechanical robustness** [N5-F3]. Solid-state electrolytes, by contrast, are often rigid and may require more complex fabrication for flexible devices, but they can avoid some of the freezing-related issues that liquid electrolytes face [N1-F1][N5-F3].

The advantages of hydrogels include:
- **flexibility and mechanical resilience**,
- **intrinsic antifreezing behavior** through network engineering [N1-F1][N4-F2],
- **additive-assisted improvements** such as glycerol and ZnCl2 [N1-F1],
- **biodegradability and biomass-based design** [N1-F1][N5-F3].

The limitations include:
- **significant conductivity loss below −40 °C** [N1-F1],
- **mechanical failure, dehydration, freezing, interfacial delamination, and irreparable damage** under repeated cycling [N5-F3],
- the need for careful tradeoffs between **flexibility, conductivity, strength, and self-healing** [N4-F2][N5-F3].

### 6) Tradeoffs necessary for subzero operation

To operate at subzero temperatures, hydrogels must make several tradeoffs:
- **Conductivity vs. freezing resistance**: antifreezing behavior often requires network design that suppresses ice crystallization, but this can reduce ion mobility unless the network is carefully tuned [N1-F1][N4-F2].
- **Flexibility vs. mechanical strength**: high water content improves flexibility but can weaken the hydrogel and promote freezing [N1-R3]; crosslinking increases strength but may reduce flexibility if overdone [N4-F2].
- **Additives vs. intrinsic antifreezing**: cryoprotectants such as glycerol or ZnCl2 can improve performance, but they may also reduce conductivity or complicate the electrolyte chemistry [N1-F1].
- **Self-healing vs. durability**: repeated cycling can cause damage, so self-healing is often necessary, but it is not a universal solution and does not eliminate all failure modes [N5-F3].

### 7) Limitations and failure modes under subzero operation

The main failure mechanisms at subzero temperatures are:
1. **Ice crystallization**, which disrupts ion transport and reduces conductivity [N1-F1][N1-R1].
2. **Mechanical damage**, including brittleness, cracking, and irreparable deformation [N1-R3][N5-F3].
3. **Interfacial degradation**, such as delamination under mechanical stress [N5-F3].

Device lifetime and safety degrade with repeated cycling because the hydrogel must repeatedly withstand freezing, thawing, and mechanical stress. The evidence shows that repeated mechanical deformation can cause **significant deformation-induced irreparable damage**, and that self-healing is essential for recovering performance [N5-F3]. The ultra-low-temperature hydrogel study reports that the assembled device can maintain stable performance under repeated mechanical deformations such as bending and loading [N1-F1], but this is still an exception rather than the general rule.

Performance benchmarks are therefore highly context-dependent. A **97.4% capacity retention after 20,000 cycles at −60 °C** is very strong evidence that some hydrogels can meet demanding performance standards at extreme cold [N1-F1]. However, this is still a high benchmark, and the evidence notes that **ionic conductivity in such systems typically undergoes an order-of-magnitude reduction below −40 °C** [N1-F1]. So, acceptable performance depends on whether the application requires **high flexibility, high conductivity, wide temperature range, or simply reliable operation over many cycles** [N1-F1][N5-F3].

### 8) Bottom line

In short, hydrogels used as supercapacitor electrolytes maintain **conductivity and flexibility at subzero temperatures** by:

- **preventing ice formation** through **tightly crosslinked polymer networks** and **bound water networks** [N1-F1][N4-F2],
- **preserving ion mobility** by keeping water in a transport-supportive state rather than freezing it [N1-F1][N4-F2],
- **enhancing mechanical resilience** with **crosslinking strategies** and **additives** such as glycerol and ZnCl2 [N1-F1][N4-F2],
- **avoiding failure modes** such as **mechanical damage, interfacial delamination, and irreversible conductivity loss** [N1-F1][N5-F3],
- and **balancing tradeoffs** between flexibility, conductivity, strength, and self-healing [N4-F2][N5-F3].

This makes hydrogels a promising but still challenging solution for subzero supercapacitors: they are not perfect substitutes for liquid or solid-state electrolytes, but they can offer a superior compromise when the hydrogel is carefully engineered for both **electrochemical stability** and **mechanical durability** [N1-F1][N4-F2][N5-F3].

However, this is still a high benchmark, and the evidence notes that **ionic conductivity in such systems typically undergoes an order-of-magnitude reduction below −40 °C** [N1-F1]. So, acceptable performance depends on whether the application requires **high flexibility, high conductivity, wide temperature range, or simply reliable operation over many cycles** [N1-F1][N5-F3].

### 8) Bottom line

In short, hydrogels used as supercapacitor electrolytes maintain **conductivity and flexibility at subzero temperatures** by:

- **preventing ice formation** through **tightly crosslinked polymer networks** and **bound water networks** [N1-F1][N4-F2],
- **preserving ion mobility** by keeping water in a transport-supportive state rather than freezing it [N1-F1][N4-F2],
- **enhancing mechanical resilience** with **crosslinking strategies** and **additives** such as glycerol and ZnCl2 [N1-F1][N4-F2],
- **avoiding failure modes** such as **mechanical damage, interfacial delamination, and irreversible conductivity loss** [N1-F1][N5-F3],
- and **balancing tradeoffs** between flexibility, conductivity, strength, and self-healing [N4-F2][N5-F3].

This makes hydrogels a promising but still challenging solution for subzero supercapacitors: they are not perfect substitutes for liquid or solid-state electrolytes, but they can offer a superior compromise when the hydrogel is carefully engineered for both **electrochemical stability** and **mechanical durability** [N1-F1][N4-F2][N5-F3].
